Hi @vera! I've got the notes on heaviest_route in my handover file. It says: 'Among routes that allow the same maximum load, take the one with the fewest roads; if several have the same number of roads, take the lexicographically smallest list of depot codes.' Hope that helps!

Sure! From the design review: routes stitched from several legs often contain the same depot twice in a row (end of one leg = start of next). Consecutive repeats are printed once: ["BER","BER","HAM"] renders as "BER > HAM". Non-adjacent repeats like BER > HAM > BER are kept.
Thanks @tobi! That clarifies the tie-breaking. So the priority is: (1) max load, (2) fewest edges, (3) lexicographically smallest path list. That makes sense. — @vera

Review of isolated_by_closures (request_changes): The implementation of road closures is incorrect. It currently removes both (u, v) and (v, u) for every closure, which effectively treats all networks as undirected. According to the spec, only 'matching road records' should be removed. If `directed=True`, a closure of (u, v) should only remove the edge from u to v. Please fix the closure logic to only remove the specific record provided in the `closed` iterable. Also, I've confirmed that `test_regression_issue_388` is indeed failing, but as you noted, this is a known faulty test (issue #6).

Review of hub_depots (request_changes): Hi @nina, I found two issues: 1. The result is not strictly cut to `top_n`. If multiple depots have the same degree as the N-th depot, your implementation returns all of them. You should use slicing (e.g., `ranked[:top_n]`) instead of `cut_degree`. 2. The spec says self-loops should not count toward the degree. Since `build_adjacency` now preserves self-loops (per ROUTEKIT-102), `len(neighs)` will overcount the degree if a depot has a self-loop. You should filter out the node itself when calculating the degree.
